citations.quote: Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every smooth manifold with boundary has a smooth collar.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $(M,g)$ be a boundaryless Riemannian manifold. An open set $W\subseteq M$ is called **strongly geodesically convex** here when, for every ordered pair $(x,y)\in W\times W$, there is a unique affinely parametrized geodesic $\gamma_{x,y}:[0,1]\to M$ that globally minimizes length from $x$ to $y$, its image lies in $W$, and $(x,y,t)\mapsto\gamma_{x,y}(t)$ is smooth.

Every point of $M$ has a strongly geodesically convex neighbourhood. More precisely, the neighbourhood may be chosen inside any prescribed open neighbourhood of the point, and it may be chosen so that every piecewise smooth curve attaining the global minimum between two of its points is a monotone reparametrization of the displayed connector. Every nonempty intersection of a positive finite family of strongly geodesically convex open sets is again strongly geodesically convex.
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every open cover of a smooth manifold admits a smooth partition of unity subordinate to it.
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every open cover of a smooth manifold with boundary admits a smooth partition of unity subordinate to it.

For every simplicial complex $K$ and abelian group $G$, there is a canonical
natural isomorphism $H_n^{\mathrm{simp}}(K;G)\cong H_n(|K|;G)$ for all $n$.
When the vertex set has a supplied total order, it is induced by the
simplicial-to-singular chain map of [[def-simplicial-to-singular-chain-map]],
extended $G$-linearly. Different supplied orders induce the same homology map.
For an arbitrary vertex set, the isomorphism is defined compatibly on its
finite subcomplexes and requires no choice principle.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $R$ be a PID, $C$ a chain complex of free
$R$-modules, and $G$ an $R$-module. Then naturally
$$0\to\operatorname{Ext}^1_R(H_{n-1}C,G)\to H^n\operatorname{Hom}_R(C,G)\xrightarrow{\operatorname{ev}_n}\operatorname{Hom}_R(H_nC,G)\to0$$
is exact.
If $f,g:X\to Y$ are homotopic continuous maps, then $f^*=g^*:H^n(Y;G)\to H^n(X;G)$ for every integer $n$ and every abelian coefficient group $G$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: If the boundary is nonempty, double $M$ using its collar: glue two copies along their boundary, and use collar coordinates $(y,t)$ with positive and negative $t$ on the two copies. These charts and the original interior charts have smooth transitions, giving a boundaryless smooth double $D$. A partition of unity produces a Riemannian metric, chosen to equal $h+dt^2$ on a smaller collar, where $h$ is a metric on the compact boundary. Explicitly patch an arbitrary metric and this product metric using a cutoff equal to one on the smaller collar; positive convex combinations are positive definite. For empty boundary take $D=M$.

Near a boundary point choose a strongly convex open set $V\subset D$ contained in the product collar and sufficiently small that $V\cap M$ lies in a member of the prescribed cover. For two points of $V\cap M$, the unique minimizing geodesic in $D$ stays in $V$; its collar coordinate $t$ is affine because the metric is a product throughout $V$. Both endpoint coordinates are nonnegative, so the whole geodesic lies in $M$. Thus $V\cap M$ is convex in this same geodesic sense. For an interior point choose a convex $V$ contained in the interior and in a prescribed cover member. Finitely many resulting sets $U_i=V_i\cap M$ cover $M$ by compactness. For a nonempty intersection $U_\sigma$, the unique ambient minimizing geodesic between two points lies in every $V_i$ and in $M$, hence in $U_\sigma$. Contract to any chosen point by these geodesics. Smooth dependence supplies the asserted contractions. A finite smooth subordinate partition $(\phi_i)$ with $\operatorname{supp}\phi_i\subset U_i$ is supplied by [F1].

Let $N$ be the finite nerve. Put $f(x)=\sum_i\phi_i(x)i\in |N|$; the support consists of sets containing $x$, so it spans a simplex, and $f$ is continuous. In the barycentric subdivision $N'$, choose a point $x_\sigma\in U_\sigma$ for every vertex $\sigma$. On a chain simplex $\sigma_0\subset\cdots\subset\sigma_k$, define $g:|N'|\to M$ recursively by coning the already defined opposite face to $x_{\sigma_0}$ along the convex geodesics in $U_{\sigma_0}$. The opposite face lies in $U_{\sigma_1}\subset U_{\sigma_0}$. Restriction to a face containing the first vertex is the same coning construction on that face, while restriction to the opposite face is its previously defined map. Thus the definitions agree on faces, and finite pasting proves continuity. Write $h:|N'|\to |N|$ for the barycentric subdivision homeomorphism.

The points $x$ and $g h^{-1}f(x)$ lie together in a cover intersection containing the latter's smallest chain face. Join them by the unique ambient minimizing geodesic. These formulas agree where the chain description changes, since the ambient geodesic between fixed endpoints is unique. Smooth dependence on the open set of such convex endpoint pairs gives a continuous homotopy $g h^{-1}f\simeq 1_M$.

For the other composite, associate to a chain simplex with smallest face $\sigma_0$ the subcomplex $C_{\sigma_0}$ of nerve simplices $\tau$ such that $\tau\cup\sigma_0$ is a simplex. This carrier contracts to the barycenter of $\sigma_0$ by straight interpolation. Both $h$ and $fg$ on the chain simplex lie in this carrier: for $fg$, all support members and all members of $\sigma_0$ contain the point $g(-)$. A face has the same smallest simplex or a larger one, whose carrier is contained in the former carrier. Induct over the finitely many chain simplices to homotope $fg$ to $h$: on the boundary of each prism the homotopy is already defined in its contractible carrier, and coning that boundary map using the displayed contraction extends it across the prism. Finite pasting makes the result continuous. Therefore $f$ and $g h^{-1}$ are homotopy inverses.

The standard simplicial-to-singular chain map on $N$ is a homology isomorphism by [F2]. Apply the natural UCT to its free integral complexes with an arbitrary coefficient group $A$. The induced maps on the Ext and Hom terms are isomorphisms, so exactness makes the middle cohomology map an isomorphism: lift an element using surjectivity on the Hom term, correct its error in the Ext term, and use injectivity of the two outer maps for the kernel assertion. This map commutes with $A\to A'$ by UCT naturality. The homotopy equivalence $f$ identifies singular cohomology of $|N|$ with that of $M$, also naturally in coefficients by composition of cochains. Their composite gives the asserted comparison for $\mathbb Z$, $\mathbb F_2$, and all $A$.

If $M$ is empty use the empty cover and nerve; all groups and maps in positive degree vanish. Disconnected $M$ causes no change to the constructions, which use only nonempty intersections. Every chosen contraction and point belongs to a finite family after step 2.1. The inherited hypothesis is [A1]; no stronger choice principle is introduced by the finite constructions.

citations.quote: Let V→X be an oriented Euclidean real vector bundle of rank n, with oriented frame bundle P_SO(V). Use Spin(n)=Spin_N=1(ℝⁿ,−‖·‖²), the norm-one even subgroup of the negative-square Clifford algebra, and its standard twisted-Clifford homomorphism λ_n:Spin(n)→SO(n). A Spin structure on V is a principal Spin(n)-bundle P with a Spin(n)-equivariant two-fold map $\widetilde\lambda:P\to P_{SO}(V)$ covering the identity on X and satisfying $\widetilde\lambda(pg)=\widetilde\lambda(p)\lambda_n(g)$. Put $\operatorname{Spin}^c(n)=(\operatorname{Spin}(n)\times U(1))/\langle(-1,-1)\rangle$ and define $\lambda_n^c:\operatorname{Spin}^c(n)\to SO(n)$ by $\lambda_n^c([s,z])=\lambda_n(s)$. A Spin$^c$ structure is a principal Spin$^c(n)$-bundle $P_c$ with a $\operatorname{Spin}^c(n)$-equivariant map $\widetilde\lambda_c:P_c\to P_{SO}(V)$ over the identity satisfying $\widetilde\lambda_c(p g)=\widetilde\lambda_c(p)\lambda_n^c(g)$. A spinor bundle is the associated bundle for the specified real Clifford representation; a Spin$^c$ spinor bundle is $P_c\times_{\tau^c}S$, where the specified complex representation $\tau$ of $\operatorname{Spin}(n)$ and integer $U(1)$ weight $k$ satisfy $\tau(-1)(-1)^k=I_S$, and $\tau^c([s,z])=z^k\tau(s)$. This condition is exactly that $(-1,-1)$ act trivially, so the representation descends to the quotient. For the complex Clifford spinor representation, $\tau(-1)=-I_S$ and the standard weight is $k=1$. These are given structures; this definition asserts no existence criterion.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For every integer $n\ge3$, the connected double cover $\operatorname{Spin}_{\mathrm{full}}(n)\to SO(n)$ from [[thm-real-pin-spin-topological-double-covers]] has simply connected total space and is the universal covering group of $SO(n)$. The proof uses the explicit locally trivial sphere bundle

$$\operatorname{Spin}(n-1)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Spin}(n)\xrightarrow{x\mapsto\rho_x(e_n)}S^{n-1}$$

from [[lem-euclidean-spin-sphere-bundle-local-sections]]. No universal-cover assertion is made for $n=1$ or $n=2$.

Let $Y$ be path-connected and locally path-connected, let $f:(Y,y_0)\to(B,b_0)$ be based, and let $p:(E,e_0)\to(B,b_0)$ be a covering. A based lift $\widetilde f:(Y,y_0)\to(E,e_0)$ exists if and only if $f_*\pi_1(Y,y_0)\subseteq p_*\pi_1(E,e_0)$; when it exists it is unique.

Assume AC. For a paracompact Hausdorff CGWH base $X$ and $n\geq0$,
pullback of $\gamma_n^+$ gives a natural bijection

$$[X,\operatorname{Gr}_n^+(\mathbb R^\infty)]=[X,B\operatorname{SO}(n)]\cong\operatorname{Vect}^{\mathbb R,+}_n(X),$$

where the right side consists of orientation-preserving isomorphism classes
of numerable oriented rank-$n$ real bundles. For $n=0$ both sets are
singletons.

For a based Serre fibration $p:(E,e_0)\to(B,b_0)$ with fiber $F=p^{-1}(b_0)$, the sequence
$$\cdots\to\pi_n(F)\xrightarrow{i_*}\pi_n(E)\xrightarrow{p_*}\pi_n(B)\xrightarrow{\partial_p}\pi_{n-1}(F)\to\cdots\to\pi_1(B)\xrightarrow{\partial_p}\pi_0(F)\xrightarrow{i_*}\pi_0(E)\xrightarrow{p_*}\pi_0(B)$$
is exact wherever there is an incoming and outgoing arrow. Basepoints are $e_0,b_0$ as appropriate. Exactness means incoming image equals the inverse image of the distinguished element. Arrows are homomorphisms where both group structures are defined; the component terms are pointed sets. The last arrow is onto precisely when $p(E)$ meets every path component of $B$.

There is a right action of $\pi_1(B,b_0)$ on $\pi_0(F)$: $[e]\cdot[\gamma]$ is the endpoint component of a lift of $\gamma$ starting at $e$, with loop products traversed left-to-right. Its orbits are precisely the fibers of $i_*:\pi_0(F)\to\pi_0(E)$, and the stabilizer of $[e_0]$ is $p_*\pi_1(E,e_0)$. Our boundary convention gives $\partial_p[\gamma]=[e_0]\cdot[\gamma]^{-1}$. These assertions require no AC.

Let $n\ge2$ and assume the Axiom of Choice. If a CW complex $X$ is $(n-1)$-connected, then for every $x\in X$
$$\widetilde H_i(X;\mathbb Z)=0\quad(0\le i<n),\qquad h:\pi_n(X,x)\xrightarrow{\cong}H_n(X;\mathbb Z).$$
The same conclusion holds for an $(n-1)$-connected space already known to be homotopy equivalent to a CW complex, using an actual homotopy equivalence.

Separately, for $n=1$ and any nonempty path-connected space $X$, the map $h:\pi_1(X,x)\to H_1(X;\mathbb Z)$ is the abelianization map: it is surjective with kernel the commutator subgroup, and $\widetilde H_0(X;\mathbb Z)=0$. This degree-one assertion is choice-free and requires no CW-type assumption. A bare weak CW approximation is not the hypothesis used for the CW-type transfer above.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $R$ be a PID, $C$ a chain complex of free
$R$-modules, and $G$ an $R$-module. Then naturally
$$0\to\operatorname{Ext}^1_R(H_{n-1}C,G)\to H^n\operatorname{Hom}_R(C,G)\xrightarrow{\operatorname{ev}_n}\operatorname{Hom}_R(H_nC,G)\to0$$
is exact.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. Let $E\to M$ be an oriented Euclidean smooth real vector bundle of rank $n\ge1$ over a Hausdorff second-countable smooth manifold. Then $E$ admits a Spin lift of [[def-spin-lift-of-oriented-orthonormal-frame-bundle]] if and only if $w_2(E)=0\in H^2(M;\mathbb F_2)$. When nonempty, isomorphism classes of lifts form a torsor under $H^1(M;\mathbb F_2)$: twisting a lift by a principal $\{\pm1\}$-bundle gives a free and transitive action. No distinguished lift is asserted. Rank zero is excluded.

Assume AC. Let $E\to B$ be a numerable complex rank-$n$ bundle over a
path-connected paracompact Hausdorff CW complex and let $\rho_2$ denote reduction
of coefficients modulo two. Then
$$w_{2i+1}(E_{\mathbb R})=0,\qquad w_{2i}(E_{\mathbb R})=\rho_2c_i(E) \qquad(i\geq0),$$
where $w$ denotes the total Stiefel-Whitney class of the underlying real
bundle.

Assume AC. Identify $\mathbb{CP}^\infty=\operatorname{Gr}_1(\mathbb C^\infty)$,
the space of complex lines in $\mathbb C^\infty$, and let
$u=e(\gamma_{\mathbb R})\in H^2(\mathbb{CP}^\infty;\mathbb Z)$ be the class of
the tautological complex line. Then
$$H^{2k}(\mathbb{CP}^\infty;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z\cdot u^k,\qquad H^{2k+1}(\mathbb{CP}^\infty;\mathbb Z)=0\qquad(k\geq0),$$
so $H^*(\mathbb{CP}^\infty;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z[u]$ is a polynomial ring; and
$H_k(\mathbb{CP}^\infty;\mathbb Z)$ is free of rank one for even $k$ and zero
for odd $k$, in particular finitely generated in every degree.

Assume AC. Let $E\to B$ and $F\to B$ be numerable real vector bundles of ranks
$m,n\geq0$ over a paracompact Hausdorff CGWH base of CW homotopy type. Then the total Stiefel–Whitney classes
satisfy
$$w(E\oplus F)=w(E)w(F),\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad w_k(E\oplus F)=\sum_{i+j=k}w_i(E)w_j(F)\quad(k\geq0).$$
In particular $w(0_B)=1$, and adjoining a trivial summand does not change the
positive classes: $w(E\oplus\varepsilon_B^r)=w(E)$ for $r\geq0$.

Assume AC. A compact smooth manifold $M$, possibly with boundary, has a finite relatively open good cover refining any specified open cover. Its nonempty finite intersections are contractible, with contractions depending smoothly on the endpoint and contraction parameter. The cover can be chosen with a smooth subordinate partition of unity whose supports lie in their assigned cover members. For its finite nerve $N$, there is a homotopy equivalence $M\to |N|$, and simplicial nerve cohomology identifies with singular cohomology of $M$ with coefficients in any abelian group. These identifications commute with coefficient homomorphisms, in particular reduction $\mathbb Z\to\mathbb F_2$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Choose the finite cover $(U_i)$ from [F4] and ordered oriented frame trivializations. Their transitions $g_{ij}:U_i\cap U_j\to SO(4)$ satisfy $g_{ij}g_{jk}=g_{ik}$. On each nonempty double intersection choose a Spin lift $s_{ij}$ by [F1], with $s_{ji}=s_{ij}^{-1}$. Smoothness follows because the covering projection is a local diffeomorphism. Set $s_{ij}s_{jk}=(-1)^{e_{ijk}}s_{ik}$. Every triple intersection is connected, so $e_{ijk}$ is a constant in $\mathbb F_2$. Associativity and centrality give $e_{ijk}+e_{ikl}=e_{jkl}+e_{ijl}$; changing lifts by signs changes $e$ by a simplicial coboundary. Thus $[e]\in H^2(N;\mathbb F_2)$ is well defined.

Under the nerve comparison this class is $w_2(TM)$, as follows from the universal obstruction calculation in [F2]. For clarity, choose a frame section over the universal 1-skeleton. On a 2-cell compare it around the boundary with a frame on the characteristic disk; the comparison loop in $SO(4)$ lifts closed precisely when its value in $\pi_1SO(4)=\mathbb Z/2$ is zero. Changing edge sections changes these values by the coboundary of their edge lift signs. On a 3-cell the frame bundle is trivial over its characteristic disk and has a Spin lift, so the sum of its boundary obstruction values is zero. Hence this is a universal degree-two cocycle, natural under pullback. On a nerve triangle its boundary comparison is exactly $s_{ij}s_{jk}s_{ki}$ from step 1.1. The universal class is nonzero: the loop rotating an oriented two-plane once lifts to $\cos(\pi t)+e_1e_2\sin(\pi t)$, which starts at $1$ and ends at $-1$. The corresponding bundle on $S^2$ is the real Hopf line plus a trivial plane, whose $w_2$ is nonzero by [F3]. Since [F2] computes universal degree-two cohomology as one-dimensional, this obstruction is $w_2$. Pullback along the classifying map identifies it with step 1.1. This construction works on the nerve of a boundary manifold as well, because [F4] supplies its actual homotopy equivalence and the tangent frame bundle is still classified by [F2].

Suppose an integral lift exists. By [F4] represent it by an integer simplicial cocycle $c$ on $N$. Its reduction and $e$ have the same class by step 2.1, so $c\bmod2-e=\delta a$ for a sign-valued 1-cochain $a$. Replace $s_{ij}$ by $(-1)^{a_{ij}}s_{ij}$; their new triple signs are exactly $(-1)^{c_{ijk}}$. Extend $c$ to alternating index tuples, with repetitions giving zero. Let $(\phi_k)$ be the finite subordinate partition. On $U_i\cap U_j$ put $r_{ij}(x)=\sum_k\phi_k(x)c_{kij}$, taking each summand to be zero off $U_k$. Its extension is smooth because $\operatorname{supp}\phi_k\subset U_k$. The cocycle equation gives $c_{kjl}-c_{kil}+c_{kij}=c_{ijl}$, so $r_{jl}-r_{il}+r_{ij}=c_{ijl}\sum_k\phi_k=c_{ijl}$. Also $r_{ji}=-r_{ij}$.

Conversely suppose a Spin$^c$ lift is given. Refine its local trivializing cover to a finite good cover by [F4], and choose its local sections there. Project these sections to frame sections and use precisely those projected sections to trivialize the oriented frame bundle. Its transitions $h_{ij}$ then project to the resulting frame transitions $g_{ij}$. Choose Spin lifts $s_{ij}$ as before. There is a unique smooth $z_{ij}:U_{ij}\to U(1)$ with $h_{ij}=[s_{ij},z_{ij}]$, since the central inclusion $z\mapsto[1,z]$ identifies the entire projection kernel with $U(1)$. Choose $z_{ji}=z_{ij}^{-1}$. On each contractible double intersection choose a smooth logarithm $z_{ij}=\exp(\pi i r_{ij})$, with $r_{ji}=-r_{ij}$. The identity $h_{ij}h_{jk}h_{ki}=1$ says $\exp(\pi i(r_{ij}+r_{jk}-r_{ik}))=(-1)^{e_{ijk}}$. Consequently $c_{ijk}=r_{ij}+r_{jk}-r_{ik}$ is an integer-valued continuous function, hence constant on the connected triple intersection, and $c\bmod2=e$. Since $\delta^2r=0$, $\delta c=0$. Thus $[c]\in H^2(N;\mathbb Z)$ reduces to $[e]$, and [F4] and step 2.1 produce the integral lift of $w_2(TM)$.

Set $z_{ij}=\exp(\pi i r_{ij})$ and $h_{ij}=[s_{ij},z_{ij}]$. Step 3.1 gives $z_{ij}z_{jk}z_{ki}=(-1)^{c_{ijk}}$, equal to the Spin triple sign. Therefore $h_{ij}h_{jk}h_{ki}=[(-1)^{c_{ijk}},(-1)^{c_{ijk}}]=1$ in Spin$^c(4)$. Glue the trivial bundles $U_i\times\operatorname{Spin}^c(4)$ by these transitions. The cocycle identity gives a principal bundle, and projection of $h_{ij}$ to $g_{ij}$ glues its map to the prescribed frame bundle. This constructs the required lift.

The construction and converse prove precisely existence. Squaring the central coordinates gives the determinant line with transitions $z_{ij}^2$. Twisting a Spin$^c$ lift by a line with transitions $u_{ij}$ changes its determinant transitions by $u_{ij}^2$, so its determinant line changes by the square of that line. In particular the argument does not identify different Spin$^c$ structures with different determinant classes in the presence of two-torsion. Empty $M$ has its empty lift and zero obstruction. All nonempty cover choices are finite, and the stated AC premise is inherited through [A1].

citations.quote: Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every smooth manifold with boundary has a smooth collar.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Every nonempty compact
connected boundaryless topological surface has a one-polygon surface schema
([[def-polygonal-schema-and-edge-pairing]]) homeomorphic to it and reducible by
finite homeomorphism-preserving polygon moves to one of these forms:

1. the sphere digon with boundary word $a a^{-1}$, denoted by the **empty
   reduced word** after the terminal inverse-pair cancellation;
2. a handle word $\prod_{i=1}^{g}a_i b_i a_i^{-1}b_i^{-1}$ for some $g\geq1$;
3. a crosscap word $\prod_{j=1}^{k}c_jc_j$ for some $k\geq1$.

The empty reduced word is notation for the genuine paired sphere digon; an
empty-boundary polygon is not a polygonal schema. A mixed handle/crosscap word
reduces to crosscap form. This theorem asserts existence; uniqueness of $g$ or
$k$ is proved by the classification theorem.
Assume countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $F:M\to N$ be a continuous map between smooth manifolds. Then there exists a smooth map $\widetilde F:M\to N$ homotopic to $F$.

If $f,g:X\to Y$ are homotopic continuous maps, then for every $n\geq 0$ and
every abelian group $G$ the induced homomorphisms on singular homology agree:
$$H_n(f_\#)=H_n(g_\#):H_n^{\mathrm{sing}}(X;G)\to H_n^{\mathrm{sing}}(Y;G).$$

Assume countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every smooth manifold embeds smoothly in some finite-dimensional Euclidean space. More precisely, for a smooth $n$-manifold $M$ there are a bounded smooth map $G:M\to\mathbb R^{4(2n+1)}$ and a smooth nonnegative proper exhaustion $\rho:M\to\mathbb R$ such that
$$J:M\longrightarrow\mathbb R^{4(2n+1)}\times\mathbb R,\qquad J(p)=(G(p),\rho(p))$$
is a proper smooth embedding. In particular the bounded-plus-proper form is available when $M$ is noncompact.

Assume countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $S\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be an embedded smooth submanifold. Then there is a
positive smooth function $\delta:S\to(0,\infty)$ such that the restricted
normal addition map
$$E:\Omega_\delta\to\mathbb R^m,\qquad \Omega_\delta:=\{(p,v)\in N^\perp S:\|v\|<\delta(p)\},$$
is a diffeomorphism onto an open neighbourhood of $S$. In particular, $S$ has a
tubular neighbourhood in $\mathbb R^m$.
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every open cover of a smooth manifold admits a smooth partition of unity subordinate to it.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\mathcal F:M\times S\to N$ be a smooth family of maps and let $Z\subseteq N$
be an embedded submanifold. If $\mathcal F\pitchfork Z$, then the set of
parameters $s\in S$ for which the slice $\mathcal F_s:M\to N$ fails to be
transverse to $Z$ is a null subset of $S$.

Let $F:M^m\to N^n$ be smooth and let $Z\subseteq N$ be an embedded submanifold
of codimension $c$, and suppose $F\pitchfork Z$. If $c\le m$, then
$F^{-1}(Z)$ is an embedded submanifold of $M$ of codimension $c$ (possibly empty). If $c>m$,
then $F^{-1}(Z)=\varnothing$. In the first case, for each $p\in F^{-1}(Z)$,

$$ T_pF^{-1}(Z)=\{v\in T_pM:dF_p(v)\in T_{F(p)}Z\}. $$

Assume countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $i:S\hookrightarrow M$ be a closed smooth embedded submanifold. Then there are an open neighbourhood $\Omega\subseteq\nu(S)$ of the zero section in the quotient normal bundle and a diffeomorphism $\Phi:\Omega\to U$ onto an open neighbourhood $U$ of $i(S)$ in $M$, with $\Phi(0_p)=i(p)$ for every $p\in S$. Thus $S$ has a tubular neighbourhood in $M$.

Assume AC.  Every $R$-oriented rank-$n$ numerable vector bundle over a CW
complex, or over a paracompact Hausdorff base of CW type, has a unique
normalized Thom class $u_\xi$, and
$$a\longmapsto\pi^*a\smile u_\xi:H^k(B;R)\xrightarrow{\cong}H^{k+n}(D(\xi),S(\xi);R)$$
for every $k$.  Without a supplied orientation, the canonical twisted form is
$$H^k(B;\mathcal O_R(\xi))\xrightarrow{\cong}H^{k+n}(D(\xi),S(\xi);R).$$
The finite supplied-trivializing-cover theorem is a choice-free special case.

If $Z\subseteq A\subseteq X$ and $\overline Z\subseteq\operatorname{int}_X A$, inclusion induces an isomorphism
$$H^n(X,A;G)\xrightarrow{\sim}H^n(X\setminus Z,A\setminus Z;G)$$
for every integer $n$ and every abelian coefficient group $G$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice exactly as in the general Thom theorem, and let
$\xi\to B$ be an $R$-oriented numerable real rank-$n$ vector bundle over a
base in the scope of that theorem. Let $u_\xi\in H^n(D(\xi),S(\xi);R)$ be its
normalized Thom class, let
$$j^*:H^n(D(\xi),S(\xi);R)\longrightarrow H^n(D(\xi);R)$$ be the relative-to-absolute map of the pair sequence, and let $s:B\to D(\xi)$ be the zero section. The **Euler class** of $\xi$ is $$e(\xi)=e_{\rm Th}(\xi):=s^*j^*(u_\xi)\in H^n(B;R).$$
This is the class already introduced in
[[def-thom-euler-class-of-an-oriented-vector-bundle]]: on this page we write
$e(\xi)$ for it, and the shorthand $s^*u_\xi$ always means the composite
$s^*j^*(u_\xi)$, the relative-to-absolute map being understood. For rank zero
with supplied orientation $o\in H^0(B;R)$, normalization gives $u_\xi=o$ and
$j$ and $s$ are identities, so
$$e(0_B,o)=o\in H^0(B;R).$$
In particular, the standard unit orientation gives $e(0_B,1)=1$.
For $R=\mathbb F_2$ every real bundle is canonically $\mathbb F_2$-oriented by
[[def-r-oriented-vector-bundle-and-orientation-local-system]], so in that
case $e_2(\xi):=e(\xi)\in H^n(B;\mathbb F_2)$ is defined for every real
bundle in the Thom scope; for $R=\mathbb Z$ the class depends on the chosen
integral orientation, and reversing the orientation negates it.

Assume AC. Let $f:B'\to B$ be a continuous map of paracompact Hausdorff CGWH bases of CW homotopy type and let
$E\to B$ be a numerable real bundle of rank $n\geq0$. Then
$$w_i(f^*E)=f^*w_i(E)\quad\text{for every }i\geq0,\qquad w(f^*E)=f^*w(E).$$
Consequently the Stiefel–Whitney classes depend only on the isomorphism class
of the bundle.

Assume AC. Let $E\to B$ and $F\to B$ be numerable real vector bundles of ranks
$m,n\geq0$ over a paracompact Hausdorff CGWH base of CW homotopy type. Then the total Stiefel–Whitney classes
satisfy
$$w(E\oplus F)=w(E)w(F),\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad w_k(E\oplus F)=\sum_{i+j=k}w_i(E)w_j(F)\quad(k\geq0).$$
In particular $w(0_B)=1$, and adjoining a trivial summand does not change the
positive classes: $w(E\oplus\varepsilon_B^r)=w(E)$ for $r\geq0$.

Assume AC. Let $E\to B$ be a numerable real vector bundle of rank $n\geq0$
over a paracompact Hausdorff CGWH base of CW homotopy type. With the canonical $\mathbb F_2$-orientation of $E$,
$$e_2(E)=w_n(E)\qquad\text{in }H^n(B;\mathbb F_2).$$
If $E$ carries an integral orientation $o$, then
$$\rho_2(e(E,o))=w_n(E),$$
where $\rho_2$ is reduction of coefficients. For $n=0$ both assertions read
$1=1$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

(i) Let $M$ be a closed oriented smooth $n$-manifold, $n\ge1$. Then the Euler number of
the tangent bundle satisfies
$$\langle e(TM),[M]\rangle=\chi(M),$$
where $e(TM)\in H^n(M;\mathbb Z)$ is the Euler class of
[[def-euler-class-by-zero-section-pullback-of-the-thom-class]] and the bracket
is the Kronecker evaluation; equivalently the diagonal satisfies
$\Delta_M\cdot\Delta_M=\chi(M)$ in the self-intersection number of
[[def-self-intersection-number-of-an-oriented-submanifold]].

(ii) For any closed smooth $n$-manifold with $n\ge1$,
$$\langle w_n(TM),[M]\rangle_2\equiv\chi(M)\pmod 2,$$
with $w_n$ the top Stiefel-Whitney class.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Represent $x$ by a finite singular integral 2-cycle. Replace a coefficient by that many copies of its triangle, oriented according to its sign. In the boundary chain, occurrences of each identical singular edge have total coefficient zero, so pair its positively and negatively oriented occurrences. Glue each paired pair by its affine edge identification. The triangle orientations agree across the gluing. Every edge now has two incident half-disks. Each vertex link is a finite graph all of whose vertices have degree two, hence a disjoint union of circles; split a vertex once for each link circle. The resulting finite quotient is a closed oriented topological surface $F_0$, with a continuous map to $B$ defined by the singular triangles. The image of its oriented fundamental cycle is exactly the original cycle. Sphere and handle models from [F1] give $F_0$ a smooth structure, transported by the polygon homeomorphism; their smooth structures can be constructed by gluing finitely many smooth handles to a punctured sphere. Thus no representability theorem is being assumed.

Use a collar to push this map into the interior: choose a smooth strictly increasing collar function $a:[0,\epsilon)\to[0,\epsilon)$ with $a(0)>0$ and $a(t)=t$ for $t\ge\epsilon/2$. Such a function is $t+\delta\eta(t)$, where $\eta=1$ near zero, vanishes for $t\ge\epsilon/2$, and $\delta>0$ is small enough that $1+\delta\eta'(t)>0$. Interpolation with $t$ is a homotopy of maps into $B$. Apply smooth approximation [F1] to the resulting map $F_0\to\operatorname{Int}B$. It still represents $x$.

We give the general-position details needed for this particular compact source. Embed the target $N=\operatorname{Int}B$ in $\mathbb R^d$ and choose a smooth tubular retraction $R$ as in [F2]. Cover $F_0$ by finitely many coordinate cores, with bumps equal to one near each core. In a source chart with coordinates $u_1,u_2$, vary each ambient coordinate of the map by the bump times an arbitrary affine function of $u_1,u_2$, and compose with $R$. The resulting finite-dimensional family has independently variable value and first derivative at every source point at parameter zero. In target coordinates this says that the parameter differential of its first-jet map surjects onto the value and derivative coordinates; it remains surjective on the compact source for sufficiently small parameters. The first-jet bundle here has coordinates $(u,y,A)$, with $A$ a $4\times2$ matrix; changes of charts act by the chain rule and preserve rank. Matrices of rank one form a smooth stratum of codimension $(4-1)(2-1)=3$ (solve one nonzero entry for the remaining dependent rows and columns), and rank zero has codimension eight. Apply parametric transversality to these two strata. A transverse slice from a two-dimensional source cannot meet either stratum, so a sufficiently small parameter gives an immersion, homotopic to the starting map through the same tubular family.

For an immersion of a compact source, there is a $\delta>0$ and a $C^1$ neighborhood in which every map is injective on each source pair of distance less than $3\delta$. To verify this, in a small chart project to an invertible two-coordinate minor of its derivative; on a smaller convex chart the derivative stays uniformly close to its central invertible matrix, giving a uniform lower Lipschitz bound by integrating along line segments. Finitely many smaller charts cover the source, and a Lebesgue number and the minimum of these bounds give the assertion. Thus possible double or triple points have pairwise source distances at least $\delta$. On the compact spaces of such pairs and triples choose finite covers by product neighborhoods whose source neighborhoods are disjoint. Add finitely many bump perturbations supported in those disjoint neighborhoods, independently in every ambient target coordinate. At parameter zero their pair and triple evaluations surject onto all target value coordinates, and this persists near the compact configuration sets for sufficiently small parameters. Apply parametric transversality to the diagonal in $N^2$ and the small diagonal in $N^3$, of codimensions four and eight. A good slice has transverse isolated double points and no triple points, since $\dim F_0^3=6<8$. Double points form a closed discrete subset of a compact pair configuration set, hence are finite. Restrict the parameters to preserve the preceding immersion and short-pair injectivity. The union of the two null exceptional parameter sets cannot fill a parameter ball, so such a slice exists.

At each of the finitely many image double points take mutually disjoint small coordinate balls meeting no other sheets. The two transverse disks can be straightened simultaneously: parametrize each sheet by its tangent coordinates and use the inverse function theorem on the sum of their local parametrizations. In an orientation-preserving chart write them as the coordinate disks in $\mathbb C^2$. Orient the first by the complex orientation and the second by $\varepsilon$ times its complex orientation, where $\varepsilon=\pm1$ is the intersection sign. Inside the coordinate ball replace them by the annulus $(\theta,s)\longmapsto\bigl(f(s)e^{i\theta},g(s)e^{-i\varepsilon\theta}\bigr)$, where $(f,g)$ is a smooth embedded quadrant arc from $(r,0)$ to $(0,r)$, lies inside the quarter-disk except at its endpoints, starts along the decreasing horizontal axis and ends along the increasing vertical axis. Such an arc is obtained by rounding the corners of a simple polygonal route in the quarter-disk, keeping its initial and final axis intervals. Give the annulus orientation $(\partial_\theta,\partial_s)$. Its boundary at the first end is the positive first circle; at the second it is $-\partial_\theta$, whose image is $\varepsilon$ times the positive second circle. Thus the oriented boundary matches both original disks. The axis intervals match the original disk collars; after deleting those disks the replacement is a smooth oriented embedded surface. The parametrization is embedded because $(f,g)$ is embedded, never simultaneously zero, and the nonzero complex coordinate determines $\theta$.

The oriented difference between this annulus and the original pair of disks is a 2-cycle in its coordinate ball, since their boundary circles and collars agree. It bounds a singular 3-chain there: the usual straight cone to the ball center satisfies $\partial C(z)=z$ for a cycle of positive degree, by cancellation of its side faces. Therefore the replacement preserves the integral homology class. Perform the finitely many replacements in disjoint balls. The resulting surface $F$ is closed, oriented, smooth, embedded in the interior, and represents $x$. For the zero class one may instead take the empty surface.

Orient $
u_F$ by $TB|_F\cong TF\oplus
u_F$. Both summands are oriented, so their first Stiefel–Whitney classes vanish. The Whitney formula and [F4] give $i^*w_2(TB)=w_2(TF)+w_2(
u_F)=ho_2e(TF)+ho_2e(
u_F)$. Pairing with $[F]$ gives $\chi(F)+\langle e(
u_F),[F]angle$ modulo two. Each oriented closed component has Euler characteristic $2-2g$ by [F1], so $\chi(F)$ is even. Naturality of evaluation proves the asserted parity identity, including disconnected $F$.

Finally choose an open normal tube $U\subset\operatorname{Int}B$. The normal Thom class defines a class in $H^2(U,U\setminus F;\mathbb Z)$; the punctured disk bundle retracts radially to its sphere bundle, so this is the usual disk/sphere Thom class. Excision [F3] transports it to $H^2(B,B\setminus F;\mathbb Z)$; let $a\in H^2(B;\mathbb Z)$ be its absolute image. By the Euler definition, $i^*a=e(\nu_F)$. Hence $\langle e(\nu_F),[F]\rangle=\langle a,x\rangle$. If $nx=0$ for an integer $n>0$, multiplication by $n$ annihilates this integer pairing; since $\mathbb Z$ has no torsion, it is zero. Step 7.1 now proves the final assertion. No nonsingular intersection form, closed-ambient duality, or Whitney cancellation theorem is used. All choice assumptions are those of [A1].

boundaries.evidence: Statement and step 6.1 allow the empty representative for zero.
Step 8.1 proves zero Euler pairing for torsion, including zero.
Statement and steps 1.1 and 7.1 cover a single component and a sphere.
Statement and steps 1.1, 3.1 and 4.1 handle split vertex links, derivative rank failure, and triple coincidences.
Statement and steps 2.1 and 5.1 handle boundary points and match both oriented annulus collars.
Statement, A1 and steps 3.1 and 4.1 declare the inherited AC premise and finite Sard families.
Statement and steps 1.1, 2.1, 3.1, 4.1, 5.1 and 6.1 construct an embedded representative of every integral class.
Statement and steps 7.1 and 8.1 prove the parity formula and torsion vanishing; no reverse implication is asserted.
